title: Russian Refining Watch
dek: Ukraine's drone campaign against Russian refining: strikes, offline capacity, and the diesel crisis.

claims.text: Russia third quarter exports of refined products plunged to a multidecade low of 1.2 million barrels per day, and although there was a slight rebound in October, these volumes are likely to fall again after a new wave of Ukrainian drone strikes against refineries, Energy Intelligence reported. In early November, diesel exports reached 325,000 barrels per day, up two thirds compared to October but nearly 60 percent lower than levels at the start of the year. In the first 10 months of the year, crude oil exports averaged 5.1 million barrels per day, a gain of 350,000 barrels per day over full year 2025, and these are poised to grow in November. Full year exports of crude and products are expected to come to 6.8 million to 6.9 million barrels per day, the fourth straight annual decline and the lowest level on record, Energy Intelligence said.

Russia's seaborne crude exports rose to their highest level since late July as Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries pushed crude that would have been processed at home into export markets, Bloomberg vessel-tracking data showed, reported by OilPrice.com on Nov 17. The 39 tankers that loaded Russian crude in the week ending Nov 15 carried 30.27 million barrels, up from 23.6 million barrels on 31 ships the previous week, and weekly exports jumped by 950,000 barrels per day to 4.32 million barrels per day, the highest since June. On a four-week average, shipments reached 3.9 million barrels per day, their highest since late July and up 280,000 barrels per day from the previous reporting period. Ukraine has attacked 13 Russian refineries since the beginning of November, Bloomberg reported, including the TAIF-NK facility in Nizhnekamsk and the Ilsky refinery in southern Russia. The four-week average value of Russian seaborne crude exports slipped to $2.45 billion per week, a seven-week low, as prices for Russia's flagship Urals crude fell for a fifth consecutive week, and Asian-bound shipments, including cargoes without confirmed final destinations, rose to 3.72 million barrels per day from 3.42 million barrels per day a week earlier.

More than a month after President Donald Trump announced the Russian diesel deal, the Agioi Fanendes was still hovering hundreds of miles off the east coast of the United States as of Sunday, Nov 15, and several other tankers that left Russia are no longer bound for the United States, CNN reported, citing MarineTraffic ship tracking data, in a report summarized by National Security Journal on Nov 16. A bipartisan group of members of Congress wrote to several major banks and port authorities shortly after the deal was announced, warning that they could face legal action if they are involved in importing Russian diesel into the United States, and that companies importing products in violation of US law may expose themselves to criminal and civil liability, CNN reported. The lawmakers questioned whether the Treasury Department's sanctions waiver was legal. A White House official told CNN that, consistent with the deal between Trump and President Vladimir Putin, Russian diesel is on the water and heading to the market, without saying the oil was coming to the United States. The Wall Street Journal reported last week that numerous ships carrying Russian diesel had either turned around or otherwise failed to deliver to the United States, and that the deal had yet to result in any new imports into the country.

Five weeks after President Donald Trump announced the Russian diesel deal on Oct 9, no delivery to a US port has been confirmed, Unbiased Headlines reported on Nov 15. Greenpeace, which tracked the fleet using shipping databases, counts six vessels carrying an estimated 268,000 tonnes of Russian diesel under the arrangement. Two tankers that left the Baltic port of Primorsk first declared US East Coast destinations and have since turned, one toward Brazil and the other into the Mediterranean, according to Kpler and MarineTraffic data, and Bloomberg and the Kyiv Post reported that the Malta-flagged Agioi Fanendes, carrying about 40,000 metric tons, reversed course roughly 400 nautical miles from New York. The US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) authorisation for Russian diesel transactions runs to Apr 7, 2027. Neither the White House nor the Kremlin has said whether the deal was put in writing, and neither has disclosed the price, payment terms or participating companies, the report said.

Kazakhstan's oil shipments through the Ust-Luga seaport have been temporarily suspended since September, so the Ukrainian drone incident at Ust-Luga on the night of Nov 11 did not affect the transportation or export of Kazakh oil, Kazakhstan Energy Ministry representative Asel Serikpayeva told journalists at Interfax-Kazakhstan, TopWar reported on Nov 12. Serikpayeva said the suspension was due to technical limitations of the transit pipeline infrastructure, that crude shipments have been rerouted to other routes so obligations to shippers and recipients are being fully met, and that export volumes from Kazakhstan have not been affected. On Nov 5, Kazakhstan's Energy Ministry contacted its Russian counterparts with a request to resume oil pumping through the Druzhba pipeline for onward shipment via Ust-Luga, and Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov said five days later that there had been no response yet.

A tanker carrying roughly 40,000 metric tons of Russian diesel was still crossing the North Atlantic on Sunday afternoon, Nov 8, with its destination listed as to be nominated, days after ship-tracking data had expected it in the New York area, Military.com reported on Nov 9. No American port has taken any Russian fuel since President Donald Trump announced the diesel deal with Moscow last month, according to tracking data and industry reporting. The Malta-flagged Agioi Fanendes loaded at Russia's Primorsk terminal on Oct 22 and initially signaled the Port of New York and New Jersey; Automatic Identification System data published by tracking service Rynda showed it still underway at about 10 knots early on Monday, Nov 9, and its manager, Eastern Mediterranean Maritime, told Reuters that no unloading port or country has been finalized. Two other tankers that loaded Russian diesel and declared US destinations have already turned, the Talisman into the Mediterranean and the Leruo toward Brazil, according to vessel tracking reported by the Associated Press and the Financial Times. New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill has warned the state's port and terminal operators that unloading such a cargo could bring civil penalties equal to the fuel's full value under the 2022 import ban.

At least six Russian diesel cargoes have broadcast that they plan transatlantic voyages to the United States under Moscow's October diesel export deal with Washington, shipping data from Kpler and LSEG showed, Reuters reported on Nov 5, while two cargoes appeared to have changed course after previously being bound for the US Atlantic coast. No Russian diesel cargo has arrived in the United States since the deal, and the first observed US-bound shipment is expected to arrive in New York this weekend, but regulatory, legislative and sanctions concerns mean its discharge is not guaranteed, Kpler analyst Matt Smith told Reuters. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the cargoes are commercial loadings whose details cannot be made public and denied any connection between tankers changing course and the US midterm election result, which President Donald Trump's Republican Party lost; Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev said Russian diesel cargoes destined for the US are continuing on course. Asked late on Thursday about a 2022 US law that could make a Russian diesel cargo illegal to land, Trump said he would take a look at it.

Russia's government has extended a general ban on diesel exports by producers until the end of January 2027 while still allowing some volumes to flow to the global market, Bloomberg reported on Oct 31 via gCaptain. The decision was taken to maintain stability in the domestic fuel market, according to a government statement announcing the signing of the relevant decree, which Bloomberg said had not yet been published. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Oct 30 that alongside the extension the government is preparing exemptions for certain suppliers to ship diesel to global markets, with similar exemptions introduced in October and planned for November. In November, Russia plans to export about 2.15 million tons of diesel after shipping about 510,000 tons in October, according to Novak, who said later that regular attacks on the nation's refineries by Ukraine may lead to a reduction in export volumes but that it would not be significant. As of late October, a total of four tankers had departed Baltic ports with Russian diesel, according to Novak.

Kazakhstan resumed oil shipments through the Atyrau-Samara pipeline on Nov 3, a day after a drone attack on the Samara Production and Dispatch Centre in Russia forced pumping to stop, the Times of Central Asia reported. Oil transportation stopped at 6:09 a.m. Astana time on Nov 2; Kazakhstan Energy Ministry spokesperson Assel Serikpayeva said that as of Nov 3 transportation through the Atyrau-Samara trunk pipeline is operating normally, after pumping resumed following a technical inspection, and the ministry reported no injuries. Atyrau-Samara is Kazakhstan's second-largest oil export route by volume, after the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC), connecting western Kazakhstan to Russia's Transneft network for onward delivery to international markets; Kazakhstan exported about 9.2 million metric tons through the route in 2025, and shipments totalled 7.573 million metric tons in the first nine months of 2026, according to KazTransOil data. The Samara hub had already come under attack, with Ukraine's General Staff saying its forces struck the pumping complex on Oct 2.

Russia's crude exports from its western ports could fall by as much as 200,000 barrels per day in November as refiners increase diesel production under Moscow's new agreement with Washington, according to preliminary loading schedules cited by Reuters on Oct 27 and reported by OilPrice.com on Oct 28. Two traders expect shipments from Russia's Baltic and Black Sea ports to decline by 100,000 to 200,000 b/d from October; the estimates include Kazakh crude transported through Russian pipelines. Russian refineries have increased processing since the October 9 diesel agreement, helped by the return of facilities from maintenance, and Moscow has issued new diesel export quotas after restricting shipments earlier this year, while Washington has eased sanctions on Russian fuel exports. Russia's seaborne crude exports averaged 3.59 million b/d in the four weeks through October 18, down 110,000 b/d from the previous period, and weekly exports fell to 3.13 million b/d, their lowest since March, following a temporary suspension of loading at Primorsk. At Novorossiysk, crude loadings are facing delays of nearly three weeks, the traders said.

Russian oil refineries increased crude processing by 25 percent in the second half of October compared with the beginning of the month, to around 5 million barrels per day, after persistent drone attacks on the plants ceased, three industry sources told Reuters on Oct 27. The sources estimated diesel production rose by at least 50,000 metric tons per day in October to 225,000 tons per day, about 1.7 million barrels per day, with about 80,000 tons per day available for export. Russian authorities said some of the last refinery attacks this month were the mid-October strikes at Ryazan and Surgut, with no further refinery strikes after October 16. The halt followed Washington's efforts to revive peace talks between Moscow and Kyiv while securing a diesel supply deal with Russia, days after which President Trump announced an energy ceasefire on October 11. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said refineries have been swiftly bringing units back online because almost all of the required oil and gas equipment is manufactured domestically. Separately, traders told Reuters on Oct 28 that crude oil exports from Russia's Baltic and Black Sea ports could fall next month as domestic refiners increase diesel output following the deal with Washington.

Russian refiners have raised diesel output for October after Moscow issued export quotas under the Kremlin's supply agreement with the United States, two industry sources told Reuters on Oct 26, in reporting by OilPrice.com. Daily production fell to about 160,000 metric tons in the first half of the month, from 175,000 tons in September, and began climbing toward 180,000 tons a day once the quotas arrived in mid-October. Russia's domestic diesel consumption typically drops to about 140,000 tons a day in October, after the grain harvest and the summer driving season end, leaving at least 40,000 tons a day, more than 1 million tons a month, available for export, according to the sources; between 200,000 and 300,000 tons of that is likely to go to neighbouring countries under intergovernmental agreements. Moscow is expected to keep its diesel export ban, which took effect in August, in place and to use quotas to control how much leaves the country. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said shipments to the United States would continue regularly, and at least two other tankers carrying Russian diesel have signaled destinations in Turkey and Brazil. Standard Chartered has warned that Russia will struggle to raise diesel output in the near term because Ukrainian drone strikes have damaged its refineries, which will take months to repair, and that barrels redirected to US buyers come out of supply to Russia's existing customers. Kyiv resumed refinery strikes on October 15 after a three-day pause, which puts the October recovery at risk.

TankerTrackers.com has identified three tankers carrying Russian diesel to the United States, all loaded at petroleum berths in Russia and declaring the USA as their destination, Robban Assafina reported on Oct 26, noting that diesel is the only known hydrocarbon that the US Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) currently permits imports of from Russia. The first cargo, on the Malta-flagged product tanker Agioi Fanendes, loaded 298,000 barrels of diesel, approximately 40,000 metric tons, at Primorsk and sailed on Oct 23; its AIS signal briefly showed New York as its destination before changing to for orders, and reported arrival dates vary between Nov 7 and Nov 10. LSEG and Kpler data show Russia has broadly resumed exports after an approximately six-week ban due to the impact of Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries, with cargoes also departed for Turkey and Brazil. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has indicated that, without further strikes, Russia would be able to resume full production by the end of the year, and diesel exports are expected to resume at a rate of 3 to 3.5 million tons per month.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Oct 23 that three tankers carrying Russian diesel are already heading toward North America, as part of a deal that could see Russia supply 500,000 metric tonnes of fuel to US and global markets in October, The Independent reported via BytesEU. Novak said the shipments have significant support from the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF). Under the deal announced by US President Donald Trump this month, Washington temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian fuel in exchange for supplies aimed at lowering global fuel prices. The first of the tankers, the Agioi Fanendes, loaded 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulfur diesel at Primorsk on Oct 22 and is expected in New York on Nov 7, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters on Oct 23.

The first tanker loaded with Russian diesel is heading for New York after Moscow agreed to resume fuel exports under the arrangement between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump, according to LSEG shipping data cited by Reuters on Oct 23 via EuropeSays. The medium-sized vessel Agioi Fanendes took on 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulfur diesel at Russia's Baltic port of Primorsk on Oct 22 and is expected to arrive in the United States on Nov 7. The US Treasury Department issued a sanctions waiver allowing the sale, delivery and import of diesel fuel, including into the United States, through April 7, 2027, and Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has indicated Russia could restore monthly diesel exports to between 3 million and 3.5 million tons by the end of the year. Russian diesel exports averaged around 345,000 b/d so far this year, down 41 percent from the previous year, according to shipping data cited by Reuters.

Russia's Transport Ministry said naval drones struck the Liberian-flagged crude tanker Aframax Rio off the resort city of Sochi on Oct 6, with crude burning openly on the Black Sea; all 23 crew, all Indian nationals, were rescued with no reported injuries. Kyiv had listed the vessel as part of Russia's shadow fleet used to move Russian oil under Western sanctions.

Overnight strikes on Oct 3-4 hit the Lazarevo pumping station on the Surgut-Gorky-Polotsk crude pipeline in the Kirov region, sparked a large fire at the Saratov refinery on the Volga, and set a fuel depot ablaze in Matveyev Kurgan; Moscow-appointed authorities in Crimea restricted gasoline sales without stating a reason.

The Black Sea export port of Novorossiysk suspended oil exports for several days after a major Ukrainian attack on the port early on Oct 2, the same Reuters-sourced reporting said, as Ukraine's campaign widened from refineries to export terminals.

Two merchant vessels were hit by air and sea drones around 3 a.m. on Oct 6 inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea, about 112 km off Byala; the Togo-flagged Alfa Watan sank with its crew missing and the Palau-flagged Able caught fire, with 18 crew rescued and two injured. Bulgarian prime minister Rumen Radev confirmed the attack, the first on shipping in Bulgarian waters, and called it a gross violation of international law; no party has claimed responsibility.

Bloomberg tanker-tracking data cited by OilPrice.com show Russia's seaborne crude exports averaged 3.62 million barrels per day in the four weeks to September 28, the highest since May 2024, a sign that neither India nor other major buyers have reduced purchases despite US pressure. Russia's oil and gas revenues were nevertheless expected to plunge 23 percent year on year in September on lower crude prices and a stronger ruble, per Reuters calculations cited in the piece.
claims.vintage: Data: four weeks ending Sep 28, 2026; accessed 2026-09-24

claims.text: The Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, the main western outlet for displaced crude, is itself constrained: trader data show exports and transit volumes more than halved from July to August, from 800,000 barrels per day to less than 355,000, after repeated drone strikes collapsed loadings and thinned tanker availability. Chartering a Suezmax tanker to India from Novorossiysk cost about $20 million by the end of August, versus about $13 million a month earlier.

More Russian regions are introducing restrictions on retail sales of gasoline and diesel following a renewed round of Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries, according to local media and the authorities, QNC News reported on Nov 20. Industry sources say the drone attacks have cut the combined crude processing volumes of Russian refineries by 45 percent since late October, tightening supplies at filling stations across the country. In Sevastopol, the governor installed by Russia, Mikhail Razvozhayev, said gasoline sales at a number of filling stations were being limited from Thursday to one full car tank and 20 litres in jerrycans, and said the measures were meant to stop people from filling canisters with hundreds of litres at a time, which had caused queues. The Siberian city of Tomsk capped sales of gasoline at 30 litres and diesel at 50 litres from last week, and on Thursday the city of Penza, about 770 kilometres southeast of Moscow, restricted gasoline sales to 50 litres and diesel to 200 litres per vehicle. At least half a dozen other regions introduced their own restrictions earlier this month, while Crimea has been among the worst hit regions and had already brought in fuel rationing before the latest strikes this week. Russia is usually a large exporter of fuel, but it was forced to turn to imports, including from India, when widespread shortages broke out in the summer, and analysts say reduced Russian refining could also affect supplies to global fuel markets and hamper the ability of Moscow to deliver on a deal to export diesel to the United States and other buyers, QNC News said.

Ukrainian drone attacks have slashed Russian oil refineries' combined crude processing volumes by 45 percent since late October, according to estimates from two industry sources in a Reuters exclusive published on Nov 18. Following near-daily drone strikes over the last 20 days, crude processing volumes have fallen to around 400,000 metric tons per day, or around 3 million barrels per day, from over 700,000 metric tons per day at the end of October. The attacks have now disrupted or halted operations at 15 of Russia's 35 major refineries, up from nine in the middle of last week, and the combined nominal capacity of refineries affected since late October stands at around 500,000 tons per day, equivalent to approximately 54 percent of the country's total primary refining capacity of an estimated 930,000 tons per day. The sources said average crude processing volumes in November remain above 500,000 tons per day, about 5 to 10 percent below September and October levels, given the gradual reduction in operating capacity. Major refineries affected include plants in Ryazan, Yaroslavl, Kirishi and the Volga region. Russia's energy ministry did not respond to a Reuters request for comment. Reduced refining could tighten global fuel markets and hamper Russia's ability to deliver on its deal to export diesel to the United States, Reuters said.

Russia is importing gasoline at scale to cover the refining shortfall, EuropeSays reported on Nov 18. According to the Helsinki-based think tank CREA, Russia imported more than 416,000 tons of gasoline by sea in August and another 234,000 tons in September, against seaborne imports between 2023 and 2025 that peaked at about 5,000 tons a month; the shipments come mainly from Morocco, India and Turkey, Business Insider reported. Belarus alone supplied more than one million tons of gasoline to Russia by rail between January and September, with a record 212,000 tons in July, and Russia has had a complete ban on gasoline exports in place since April. On Tuesday, Nov 17, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak instructed his staff to expand gasoline imports further and to secure additional fuel that falls below Russia's emissions standard. The refineries in Yaroslavl and Nizhny Novgorod are reportedly at a standstill, Ryazan is running at only about 10 percent of capacity and Omsk, the country's largest refinery, is operating at about half capacity, according to Michael Bohnert, an analyst at RAND, and the refineries hit account for about 55 percent of Russia's gasoline production, according to Sergey Vakulenko at the Carnegie Endowment. At least eight regions are reporting fuel shortages and at least six have imposed sales caps, mostly 30 litres a day, while Rosneft stations in Moscow are limiting drivers to 50 litres per vehicle and 20 litres per canister, the report said.

Ukrainian drones have struck 11 Russian oil refineries since Oct 30, on flights of up to nearly 3,000 kilometres, and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Nov 15 that Ukraine had neutralised more than 55 percent of Russia's refining capacity, YAC News reported, citing the Kyiv Independent. Zelenskyy gave the figure in his evening address, citing a report by Major General Mykhailo Drapatyi, and called the campaign Ukraine's long-range sanctions and a fitting response to Russia's refusal to de-escalate. Ukraine's Defence Ministry had put the share at 51 percent on Oct 4. Sergey Vakulenko, a former Gazprom Neft analyst now at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in Berlin, wrote on Nov 13 that the refineries attacked in the current wave make about 55 percent of Russia's commercial petrol, and estimated that Russia's petrol stocks would last about a week of national consumption. Rosneft began limiting fuel sales at its filling stations in every Russian region by Nov 9, with drivers in Karelia and Buryatia held to 30 litres of petrol a visit in the cities, the report said. The 55 percent figure is a Ukrainian claim covering capacity neutralised, not a confirmed measure of current lost throughput, and no operator or Russian official figure reconciles with it in the reporting here.

A campaign tally published on Nov 14 counted successful Ukrainian drone attacks on Russia's six largest refineries between Oct 30 and Nov 12: Omsk, Kirishi, Ryazan, Kstovo, Yaroslavl and Volgograd. The six facilities together carry nominal capacity of 123.2 million tonnes of crude a year, representing about half of Russia's annual refining output, the tally said. Across the last 15 days it counted 13 refineries and oil and gas infrastructure facilities successfully attacked, including two attacks on the Samara loading and dispatch station and an attack on the port and transshipment facilities at Ust-Luga. The tally cautioned that a successful attack does not immediately indicate that all production at a plant has been knocked offline, and that Russia now treats shutdown and restart information as a state secret, so information on shutdowns and restarts lags weeks behind.

Russia and Ukraine agreed to a large exchange of prisoners of war as two days of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi concluded on Wednesday, Nov 11, with no major breakthrough on ending the war, the Associated Press reported. US envoy Jared Kushner said the two sides had agreed to the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, with the numbers to be finalised on Thursday, and that he and envoy Steve Witkoff would travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet President Vladimir Putin and then to Dublin to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Russian delegation head Vladimir Medinsky and Ukrainian delegation head Rustem Umerov confirmed the planned exchange, which could take place in the next two or three weeks. The talks, the first such meeting since February, lasted just under two hours on Wednesday after a four-hour session the previous day, and US mediators said differences remained on other major issues, including territory.

Renewed Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries since late October have reduced Russia's oil refining capacity by about 30 percent, two industry sources told Reuters in an exclusive published on Nov 10. Ukrainian attacks disrupted operations and caused emergency situations at nine of Russia's 35 major refineries over the past week, according to the sources and officials. The combined daily nameplate capacity of refineries affected since late October, including three major plants in central Russia, stands at around 300,000 metric tons, or 2.2 million barrels per day, compared with total primary refining capacity of about 930,000 tons per day, and at the end of October Russian refineries were processing about 700,000 tons, or 5 million barrels, of crude per day, the sources said. They estimated the actual reduction in crude processing could be up to 200,000 tons per day, with affected plants including refineries in Ryazan, Yaroslavl and the Volga region. The same report said a Ukrainian drone struck the Kirishi refinery on Monday, Nov 9, setting it on fire, and that Governor Alexander Drozdenko said one woman had been killed in the attack, a casualty not reported in the initial Nov 9 coverage on this page. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said in an article published on Tuesday in Kommersant that Ukraine was ignoring Trump's calls to stop strikes on Russian energy targets.

Three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States opened in Abu Dhabi on Nov 10, the first such meeting since February, the Associated Press reported. The two-day session will focus on security guarantees, the White House said before the discussions. US envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are mediating; Ukraine's delegation is led by Rustem Umerov, head of its Foreign Intelligence Service, and Russia's by presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky. Kushner said he believed there were some good ideas to bridge the differences between the two sides, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Monday night that he did not have overly high expectations for the talks. The two sides remain far apart: President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to pull its troops back from the four regions Moscow annexed in September 2022 and to abandon its bid to join NATO, while President Volodymyr Zelensky rejects ceding territory Russia has not taken and rejects limits on Ukraine's military. The talks took place against a backdrop of new long-range strikes, with Ukraine saying Russia launched 162 drones and a ballistic missile overnight and Russia saying it shot down 155 Ukrainian drones overnight.

Reuters reported on Nov 9 that Russia's Kirishi oil refinery was set on fire after a Ukrainian drone attack on the region on Monday, citing Governor Alexander Drozdenko. Cornerstone Futures reported the same morning that the fire broke out and has been contained, that 113 drones were downed over the region, and that Kirishi processes 400,000 barrels per day, making it one of Russia's largest refineries, producing diesel, gasoline and fuel oil mainly for export. Surgutneftegas, the owner, had not commented, and Ukrainian military officials had not either, Cornerstone said, adding that Bloomberg notes Ukraine is striking Russian energy assets almost daily. The strike landed on the eve of US mediated working level talks between Ukraine and Russia due in Abu Dhabi on Nov 10 to 11, with Reuters reporting Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will lead the US side, the Baltic Security Monitor said.
claims.source: Reuters (via Euronext Live); Cornerstone Futures; Baltic Security Monitor

claims.text: A weekly brief published on Nov 8 by Vigil Consilium, covering Nov 1 to Nov 7, grouped the latest refinery hits as three more refineries reached in one week: a fire at Lukoil's NORSI refinery in Kstovo overnight into Nov 1, a fire at the Afipsky refinery in Krasnodar Krai overnight into Nov 6, and the Saratov refinery set ablaze overnight into Nov 7. The brief said the records count reported strikes, not damage or lost throughput. It also noted Russia extended its producer diesel export ban to Jan 31, 2027. The Kstovo identification rests on monitoring channels and a statement by the drone maker Fire Point, with the Nizhny Novgorod governor reporting significant damage at an industrial facility in Kstovo district that he did not name; at Afipsky, regional authorities confirmed a fire at an unnamed enterprise and blamed drone debris.

The Yanos refinery in Yaroslavl stopped all crude processing after a Nov 3 drone attack, Bloomberg reported on Nov 6 via Briefs, citing a person familiar with the matter. Bloomberg counted six Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries since Oct 30, with Afipsky, at about 180,000 barrels a day, the most recent at the time of that report, and said this year's attacks have pushed Russian refinery throughput to multiyear lows and led Moscow to curb exports of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel. ForteInvest, the private owner of Afipsky, did not answer a Bloomberg request for comment, and regional emergency workers reported an unspecified location in the Afipsky area ignited after falling drone debris. No operator statement confirming the Yanos halt was published in the reporting here.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Nov 6 that the operation against the Russian oil refining industry continues, in a statement on Telegram issued after receiving a military command report on deep strikes, Signal Post News reported, citing Reuters. Zelenskyy said the campaign is continuing in response to Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy facilities, that new countermeasure targets had been determined, and that Russia has refused de-escalation steps. In his nightly video address the same day, he said Ukrainian intelligence indicates Russia is preparing new strikes on energy, on bridges across the Dnipro and on civilian infrastructure. The statements land four days before United States, Russia and Ukraine talks resume in Abu Dhabi on Nov 10 and 11, and a day before the reported overnight strike on the Saratov refinery.

On Nov 4 the European Commission hosts a meeting in Brussels of European Union (EU), US and Ukrainian representatives at national security adviser level, joined by France, Germany, Britain, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) and the World Bank, the Baltic Security Monitor reported. US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff set out the agenda as security guarantees for Ukraine, Europe's post-war security architecture and economic opportunities in reconstruction, building on earlier rounds in Miami and Oslo. Separately, Witkoff announced US-mediated working-level talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi on Nov 10 and 11. The monitor said the meeting is confirmed by the Commission and NATO, with no outcomes available at snapshot time. A scheduled meeting is not a commitment or a deployment, and only signed documents and concrete decisions settle what it produces.

The United States will bring together delegations from Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi on Nov 10 and 11 to discuss ending Moscow's war against Ukraine, post-war security agreements and de-escalation, Reuters reported on Nov 3. The planned talks sit alongside the resumed Ukrainian strike campaign on Russian refining: Reuters noted the same day that a Ukrainian drone attack damaged an oil refinery in the Russian city of Yaroslavl, while Russia launched a massive overnight strike on Ukrainian energy facilities in the Vinnytsia, Dnipropetrovsk and Kharkiv regions, according to Interfax, citing the Russian defence ministry.

The brief respite Russian refiners received from Ukraine appears to have ended, ING reported on Nov 2. Attacks on Russian refiners resumed towards the end of last week after a roughly two-week pause, during which the ICE gasoil crack fell below $70 a barrel and traded to its lowest level since early October. ING said further attacks would likely provide a floor to the crack, with strikes casting doubt over how much diesel Russia will export. Russia's deputy prime minister said Russia plans to export 2.15 million tonnes of diesel in November, up from a little more than 500,000 tonnes in October. ING also noted vessels have faced a growing number of attacks in recent weeks, yet this coincides with signs that more traffic is flowing through the Strait of Hormuz, and that OPEC+ members decided over the weekend to keep December output targets unchanged, with most members producing well below target given disruptions in the Persian Gulf.

Ukrainian drone strikes targeted three major Russian oil refineries over three consecutive nights, hitting facilities that together account for approximately 10 percent of Russia's total oil refining capacity, UNITED24 Media reported on Nov 1, citing Ukrainian monitoring group Dnipro Osint. The attacks targeted the Novokuibyshevsk refinery in the Samara region overnight on Oct 30, the Bashneft-Novoil facility in Ufa on Oct 31, and the Lukoil refinery in Kstovo, in the Nizhny Novgorod region, overnight into Nov 1, with a combined annual processing capacity of approximately 33 million metric tons of crude oil. The figure represents the share of capacity targeted, rather than independently confirmed production losses, and the full extent of damage has not been independently verified. Ukrainian defence manufacturer Fire Point confirmed its involvement in the strikes on the Kstovo and Novokuibyshevsk refineries, saying Ukrainian forces used FP-1 drones to target Novokuibyshevsk, striking multiple locations including a diesel hydrotreating unit. The renewed attacks followed a reported two-week pause in Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil refineries.

Three strikes in three days, Novokuibyshevsk on Oct 30, Ufa on Oct 31 and Kstovo overnight into Nov 1, look like a resumed campaign against Russian refining after a lull from mid-October, the Baltic Security Monitor reported on Nov 1. The fire at the Bashneft-Novoil refinery in Ufa is now backed by geolocated footage, not just eyewitnesses, and Ukraine's Strategic Communications Center named Bashneft-Novoil and Bashneft-Ufaneftekhim as targets. The monitor noted that the gap between visible fire and lost refining capacity remains open: damage to the L-35 unit is known only from visual analysis and is unverified, and involvement of the second Ufa plant has no geolocated evidence.

Ukraine's military has paused its strikes on Russian oil refineries after pressure from US President Donald Trump, the Wall Street Journal reported on Oct 29, citing people with knowledge of the operations, Reuters reported. Ukrainian units carrying out long-range strikes were told in mid-October that the campaign against refineries was effectively on hold once missions already in motion were completed, the Journal reported. The unofficial pause is expected to last until after the US midterm elections and potentially deeper into November, it added. Reuters could not immediately verify the report. The pause report landed a day before a reported fire at the Novokuybyshevsk refinery in the Samara region on Oct 30, the first reported refinery strike since mid-October.

JPMorgan analysts said in a note cited by Reuters on Oct 29 that since the October 15 strike on the Ryazan refinery, there have been no further confirmed attacks on Russian refining infrastructure, and that the silence has allowed Russian refinery runs to rebound by 350,000 b/d last week to 4 million b/d. Higher runs would also allow Russia to lift crude production by a broadly comparable amount, reversing part of the recent decline that pushed output to 8.4 million b/d, its lowest level since 2003, the analysts said, but higher crude production would not necessarily translate into higher crude exports. The JPMorgan run figure uses a different basis from the roughly 5 million b/d for the second half of October reported by Reuters industry sources on Oct 27, and the two are not directly comparable.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine is ready to stop strikes on Russian oil refining infrastructure if Russia refrains from attacking Ukraine's power grid, in an interview with Alla Mazur of TSN.Tyzhden reported by Ukrinform via EuropeSays on Oct 26. Zelensky said he had proposed the energy ceasefire approach to international partners, and that Ukraine is responding to Russian strikes on its energy infrastructure because Russia must also feel the consequences of its attacks. He also said Ukraine, the United States and Russia have agreed to hold a trilateral meeting at the level of negotiating teams in the first half of November.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed on Oct 24 that negotiating teams from Ukraine, Russia and the United States may meet in Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates in November, EA WorldView reported. Zelensky told the Hudson Institute in a video call, after speaking with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, that the plan is to meet in the first half of November and as early as possible, that technical-level talks would come first and a leaders summit would follow if they prove productive, and that it all depends on the Russians, noting an expected October meeting did not happen. The update follows Witkoff's meetings with Zelensky and European leaders in Oslo and with President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg earlier in the week.

Ukraine has not struck Russian oil refineries for more than a week, SFG Media reported on Oct 24. The last known refinery incident occurred overnight on Oct 16, when reports emerged of an attack on the Ryazan refinery. Kyiv resumed attacks on Russian oil-refining infrastructure on Oct 14, that day seeing strikes on two refineries for the first time after a prolonged lull, following talks between Ukrainian and American delegations in Miami on Oct 10 at which, according to media reports, Washington demanded that Kyiv halt attacks on Russian oil refineries as part of the diesel agreement between the United States and Russia. Reports of further refinery attacks ceased again two days after the apparent start of the new wave, SFG Media said. The Oct 24 strike on the Togliattikauchuk petrochemical plant in Togliatti was a petrochemical target, not a refinery.

Russia said on Oct 22 that it was ready to resume US-mediated talks with Ukraine next month, after President Vladimir Putin hosted US envoy Steve Witkoff for talks in St. Petersburg, Reuters reported on Oct 23. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said he hoped negotiations, which would be the first since February, will take place early in November.

US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff urged Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct 21 to consider resuming US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine and to review new ideas on ending the war, Reuters reported. The talks in St. Petersburg, the ninth time Witkoff has met Putin in person, began with Russia releasing Stephen Hubbard, a retired US school teacher held in Russia. Putin also offered to help US President Donald Trump in dealing with Iran, saying Russia had a decades-long relationship with Tehran which it has repeatedly offered to leverage to address US concerns about Iran's nuclear programme, and said Russia could also supply large quantities of fertiliser to the United States.

Ukraine is launching larger and deeper drone assaults on Russian refineries, storage sites and export facilities after ending its brief adherence to the energy ceasefire that President Donald Trump declared on Oct 11, CNBC reported via TradersUnion on Oct 21. State media reports say more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones targeted Russia on Sunday alone, and one of the strikes set an oil export terminal in St. Petersburg on fire. Kpler data show Russia's diesel exports fell more than 75 percent to 141,000 b/d in September from 608,000 b/d in the same period last year, and total diesel exports were around 345,000 b/d so far this year, down 41 percent. Tatiana Mitrova at Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy said the scale, range and effectiveness of the strikes have crippled Russian diesel exports, while Kpler's Matt Smith said Trump's arrangement with Putin to increase shipments is likely no longer workable without an energy ceasefire.

Russian diesel cargoes are returning to their main previous customers following the US-brokered lifting of Moscow's export ban, with at least two tankers signalling voyages to Turkey and Brazil in recent days, Reuters reported on Oct 20, citing shipping data from Kpler and LSEG. The tanker Leruo is signalling Manaus, Brazil, after departing the Baltic port of Primorsk on Oct 16, following the tanker Dolunay, which left Primorsk with a diesel cargo on Oct 14 bound for Alanya, Turkey. Turkey has received about 34 percent of Russian diesel loadings so far this year at 95,000 b/d and Brazil about 24 percent at 66,000 b/d, Kpler data show. Russia partially lifted the diesel export ban starting Oct 10; it had reduced exports over the summer before imposing the ban as it grappled with widespread Ukrainian attacks on its oil refineries.

Russia's crude oil production increased by 65,000 b/d in September to 8.43 million b/d, but remained about 870,000 b/d below a year ago, Reuters reported on Oct 20, citing the International Energy Agency's assessment published last week. The year-on-year shortfall sits alongside the refinery outage campaign and the diesel export disruption tracked on this page.

Oil prices fell on Oct 19 as traders weighed possibly higher Russian supplies after US sanctions relief on Friday, Reuters reported, with Brent crude futures down $2.29, or 2.08 percent, to $107.57 a barrel and US West Texas Intermediate down $1.95, or 1.92 percent, to $99.46, both pulling back from five-month highs settled on Friday. The waiver follows the deal Trump struck with President Putin for Russia to export diesel to the United States and other countries, starting at about 2.3 million barrels this month before rising to about 7.6 million barrels monthly, Reuters said, adding that Zelenskiy said the US actions will hurt Ukraine and that analysts said mixed messaging on the waiver's details and duration has created uncertainty, so the market is unlikely to fully price in a sustained increase in supply.

President Trump's waiver of Russian sanctions eases energy concerns for India, one of the top importers of Russian oil, and may improve the chances of New Delhi and Washington agreeing on a trade deal, Reuters reported on Oct 19. The Graham Act legislation would have exposed Indian goods to tariffs of up to 100 percent, as India is one of the five largest importers of Russian oil. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who arrives in India on Tuesday, said trade talks with New Delhi were a consideration for Trump's waiver decision and that the two sides are very close to finalising a trade deal. Earlier this year Russia accounted for nearly half of India's oil imports, but purchases fell in August and continue to decline, Reuters said.

President Trump said on Oct 17 that he had not announced a final decision on the Russia sanctions he waived a day earlier, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the president will take up to 60 days to weigh the economic impact before deciding what comes next, Reuters reported. The Oct 16 executive order used the Graham Act's waiver power to set aside most of the law's new sanctions and its duties, a 500 percent duty on Russian goods and 100 percent duties on goods from the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, which were due to take effect Oct 18; sanctions imposed under earlier executive orders remain in place, and Zelenskyy condemned the waiver.

Putin's investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev said on Oct 16 that the US Treasury has asked Russia's sovereign wealth fund, the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), which he heads, to facilitate payments relating to the Trump-Putin deal on the sale of Russian diesel. Dmitriev told an energy conference the Treasury had requested RDIF to facilitate payments and solve tactical issues, and said RDIF will work to ensure that all payments are efficient and reach their intended recipients.

Russia publicly acknowledged the Oct 15 Ukrainian drone strike on the Ryazan refinery on Oct 16 and state TV channel Rossiya-24 broadcast images of the aftermath, the first time state television has shown a refinery attack since the war began, Reuters reported. Moscow is highlighting an attack President Trump has called a disgrace, four days after he announced an energy ceasefire that neither side confirmed; Ukraine said it paused strikes for three days and resumed because Russia kept hitting Ukrainian energy infrastructure, leaving 600,000 people without power on Oct 14.

Attacks on Russian refineries have cut an estimated one million tonnes a month of fuel oil supply, Vitol's Asia head Kieran Gallagher said at the SIBCON conference this week, while high-sulphur fuel oil flows through Hormuz, including Iranian supplies, remain down by at least 800,000 tonnes a month from February. Spot premiums for 380-cst high-sulphur fuel oil held near $50 a tonne this week, versus a $5.10 premium on Feb 27, on LSEG data.

Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian refineries on Oct 15 after a three-day pause, President Zelenskiy told the Financial Times, saying the block on energy strikes was over because Russia kept hitting Ukrainian energy infrastructure, leaving 600,000 people without power on Oct 14. The Ryazan hit was the first Ukrainian attack on a Russian energy facility since President Trump announced an energy ceasefire on Oct 11, a truce neither side confirmed; Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said no specific agreements had been established.

The IEA said on Oct 14 that a lack of operational Russian refinery capacity meant the recently announced easing of Russian diesel export restrictions was unlikely to bring any material change to the global gasoil balance, and that constrained diesel supplies could persist well into next year. The agency put Russian crude production in September at 8.43 million b/d, up 65,000 b/d on the month but 870,000 b/d below a year earlier.

President Zelenskiy said on Oct 13 that Ukraine had carried out no strikes on Russian oil refineries or other energy sites in the two days since the Oct 11 US announcement of an energy ceasefire, while accusing Russia of continuing to hit Ukrainian energy facilities over the same period.

President Zelenskiy said on Oct 12 that Russia had hit at least six Ukrainian energy targets in overnight strikes despite the energy ceasefire announced by President Trump, and that Moscow had shown no interest in accepting it. The Kremlin was reported as saying it does not want a ceasefire. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, Moscow's point man for oil, said Russia would be able to return diesel exports to levels above those outlined in the Trump diesel deal.

On Oct 11 Trump posted that an 'energy ceasefire' between Russia and Ukraine was effective immediately, with neither government confirming any deal. Zelensky said Ukraine would honor it if Russia reciprocated, but Russian strikes on Ukrainian power facilities continued afterward and the Kremlin made no public commitment.

Axios, citing a US official, reported Trump moved ahead with the Russian diesel waiver after Zelensky ignored about six US requests to stop hitting Russian refineries; during Oct 9 talks in Miami, envoys Witkoff and Kushner told Ukraine's delegation the waiver was coming because the strikes were 'directly affecting U.S. consumers'.

President Trump said after a phone call with Vladimir Putin that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by 500,000 tons in November, 1 million tons 'immediately thereafter,' and 3 million more 'within a short period.' Treasury immediately issued a general license sparing Russian diesel loaded as of Oct 9 from sanctions until April 2027, the first diesel easing longer than the standard 30-day window; Deputy PM Novak told Tass Russia is lifting diesel export restrictions ahead of schedule, with US-bound supplies possible in October. The IEA says Russian diesel output has fallen about 30% amid the strikes.

Russia's State Duma budget and tax committee backed draft Tax Code amendments extending an existing fuel-import subsidy to large-scale seaborne gasoline imports from India, with the subsidy calculated off an indicative Indian gasoline price plus shipping costs. Operating refineries are producing about 85,000 tonnes of gasoline per day against demand of around 111,000 tonnes, leaving a structural shortfall near 25,000 tonnes a day, roughly 20% of consumption.
claims.source: Investment Guru India (via Kyiv Post, citing RBC)

claims.text: In a rare acknowledgment at the Oct 1 Valdai Club session, Putin said Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries had cost Russia roughly 1% of GDP and conceded Kyiv had partially achieved its goal of damaging the economy, while offering no ceasefire and saying Russia would prefer talks.

Ukraine's General Staff confirmed on Friday, Nov 20, that Ukrainian forces struck the Kaleykino oil pumping station in Russia's Tatarstan Republic on Nov 19, damaging three large oil storage tanks, the Kyiv Independent reported, via EuropeSays. According to the General Staff, Ukrainian forces struck three oil storage tanks at the Kaleykino-1 facility, with one catching fire and two others sustaining damage, and each tank has a capacity of 50,000 cubic meters of oil, making them among the largest storage facilities of their kind in Russia. The station, located near the city of Almetyevsk, more than 1,000 kilometres from the Ukrainian front line, receives and blends crude oil from different Russian regions before distributing it to refineries and the Druzhba pipeline system, which carries Russian oil to European markets, and the extent to which the attack disrupted the station's operations remains unclear. The Ukrainian military also provided updated information on an earlier strike against the Ilsky oil refinery in Russia's southern Krasnodar Krai on Nov 18: Ukrainian strikes destroyed one 5,000-cubic-meter oil storage tank and damaged eight others, including seven tanks of the same capacity and one smaller 1,000-cubic-meter tank, and the attacks also damaged a section of an oil pipeline, five technical buildings and a warehouse, with the full extent of the damage still being assessed. Ukrainian drones previously targeted the Kaleykino station in February 2026, when the strike reportedly caused a fire and disrupted oil transportation through the facility.

Ukrainian drones reportedly struck the PJSC Dorogobuzh chemical plant in Russia's Smolensk Oblast overnight on Nov 20, with explosions and a large fire seen emanating from the plant just after midnight, Telegram monitoring channels reported, via the Kyiv Independent. Monitoring channel Exilenova Plus reported the explosions and fire, and an OSINT analysis conducted by monitoring channel ASTRA concluded that the Dorogobuzh chemical plant was the target of the attack. The plant produces fertilizers, ammonia and other nitrogen-based chemicals and components linked to Russia's war machine, and the facility has been previously targeted by Ukrainian attacks on several occasions, including as recently as February 2026. The Kyiv Independent said it could not immediately verify the reports, Ukraine's military had not yet commented on the reported attack, and the extent of the damage caused was not immediately clear. The target is a chemical plant, not an oil refinery, and it is logged here as part of the same overnight strike wave, one night after Ukrainian drones struck an oil pumping station in Russia's Tatarstan Republic.

Ukrainian drones reportedly struck the Kaleykino oil pumping station in Russia's Republic of Tatarstan early on Thursday, Nov 19, targeting a key hub in the country's trunk oil pipeline network around 1,300 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, EuropeSays reported, citing the Kyiv Post and the independent Russian outlet Astra. Tatarstan authorities confirmed a Ukrainian drone attack on oil storage tanks near Almetyevsk, with the press office of Tatarstan's head Rustam Minnikhanov saying enemy drones attacked the southeastern part of the republic and that debris damaged several civilian structures, with no deaths or injuries reported; an automatic fire-extinguishing system helped contain the blaze quickly. The Kaleykino station, owned by state pipeline operator Transneft, is a major blending hub for crude arriving from Western Siberia, Tatarstan, Udmurtia and Bashkortostan, and manages distribution including supplies entering the Druzhba pipeline. Russia's Defense Ministry said its air defenses intercepted and destroyed 53 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones between 8 p.m. Moscow time on Nov 18 and 8 a.m. on Nov 19. Separately, Ukraine's Defense Forces struck the Afipsky and Ilsky oil refineries in Krasnodar Territory overnight on Nov 18, for the second time this November: Ukraine's General Staff said explosions and smoke were reported near the Ilsky refinery, where storage tanks were hit, and that an oil processing unit was reportedly struck at the Afipsky facility; the two refineries have a combined annual processing capacity of approximately 13 million tons of crude oil and supply fuel to Russian forces in the south.
claims.source: EuropeSays (citing the Kyiv Post and Astra)

claims.text: Two industrial facilities in Krasnodar Krai caught fire after a drone attack that injured four people, regional authorities said on Wednesday, Nov 18, with media identifying the targets as two major oil refineries, EuropeSays reported, carrying Moscow Times reporting. The Krasnodar region's emergency centre said falling drone debris sparked fires at two facilities and that the four injured were receiving medical treatment. The exiled outlet Astra said local residents named the targeted sites as the Afipsky and Ilsky oil refineries in Seversky district. The Afipsky refinery has a processing capacity of 9.1 million tons of crude per year and the Ilsky refinery a design capacity of over 6 million metric tons per year, and both have been attacked multiple times. Four more residents of the neighbouring republic of Adygea were hospitalised after a drone attack on a settlement less than 10 kilometres from the Afipsky refinery. Russia's Defence Ministry said it had intercepted 183 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight. Regional authorities did not name the facilities, so the refinery identifications rest on residents and monitoring channels, not on an official confirmation.

Two oil refineries in Krasnodar Krai were reportedly targeted in an overnight drone attack on Nov 17 to 18, with Ukrainian monitoring channels reporting strikes on both facilities, EuropeSays reported, carrying Kyiv Independent reporting. The monitoring channel Exilenova+ posted that the Ilsky and Afipsky refineries had both been hit, citing local sources, and Supernova+ also reported an attack on the Ilsky refinery. The Kyiv Independent said it could not independently verify the reported strikes or damage at either facility, and Ukrainian military officials did not immediately confirm the latest reported strikes. Ukraine's General Staff had previously reported striking the Ilsky refinery on Nov 16, targeting several oil-processing units and a gasoline production complex, and the Afipsky refinery was also reportedly targeted on Nov 6, when regional authorities confirmed a fire at an industrial enterprise but did not identify the facility.

Ukrainian drones struck one of Russia's largest petrochemical complexes in Bashkortostan overnight on Nov 17, triggering a major fire in the industrial city of Salavat, EuropeSays reported. The overnight attacks targeted Salavat and the regional capital Ufa, according to Bashkortostan's emergency situations committee, and Russian authorities said air defences, industrial security teams and mobile fire groups shot down more than 50 drones. Videos filmed by local residents and reviewed by the independent Russian outlet Astra suggest the strike hit Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat, which operates oil-refining and gas-chemical plants producing gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and fuel oil, and which previously was struck on Oct 8. Residents reported explosions and a blaze in Salavat's industrial zone, with the fire's glow reportedly visible from Sterlitamak, about 17 kilometres away. Russia's Defence Ministry claimed it had intercepted 1,441 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones overnight across 21 regions, occupied Crimea and the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, a figure that, if confirmed, would be a record; Russian authorities had not officially confirmed damage at the Salavat complex in the report.

Ukraine hit the road and rail bridge connecting Crimea to Russia's Krasnodar region and targeted oil refineries overnight into Monday, Nov 16, in what Russian defence ministry data showed was the biggest overnight drone attack on Russia since the start of the full-scale war in 2022, Reuters reported. Russia said its air defences brought down 1,336 Ukrainian drones across 16 regions, surpassing the 1,254 registered as shot down on Oct 29, and Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said about 600 drones had been launched at the Moscow region since Sunday evening, 191 of them brought down. The Russian-backed governor of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said the Kerch Strait bridge was struck overnight; the Kremlin called the damage minor, road traffic was temporarily suspended while repairs were undertaken, and rail traffic continued as normal, the transport ministry said. In the Krasnodar region, local officials said a fire broke out at an unnamed industrial facility in Ilsky, home to an oil refinery, and that falling drone debris injured six people, including children. Rostov region governor Yuri Slyusar said fires broke out at four industrial sites in Azov after the attack. The extent of any halt to processing at Ilsky had not been confirmed in the reporting here.

Russia's defence ministry said its air defences brought down 1,336 Ukrainian drones overnight into Monday, Nov 16, one of the largest totals of the year, over the Moscow region, Crimea, Krasnodar Krai and the Black and Azov seas, YAC News reported on Nov 16. Fires broke out at four production sites in Azov, in Rostov region, and three men were injured, Governor Yuri Slyusar said; witness footage showed an oil depot and a gas distribution station burning, the independent Russian channel Astra reported. Krasnodar Krai's emergency headquarters said a fire had broken out at an enterprise in the village of Ilsky and that falling debris had injured three people in Seversky district, among them a child. The village is home to the Ilsky refinery, one of the largest in southern Russia at about 6.6 million tonnes of crude a year, which Ukraine's General Staff says supplies the Russian armed forces. Ukraine had not confirmed a strike on the Ilsky plant by the morning of Nov 16, and neither the extent of damage at Azov nor any halt to Ilsky processing had been confirmed in the reporting here.

Ukrainian forces struck two facilities in Nizhnekamsk, in Russia's Republic of Tatarstan, overnight on Nov 15, hitting the Nizhnekamskneftekhim petrochemical complex and the TAIF-NK oil refinery, Ukraine's General Staff said. Explosions and a fire were reported at Nizhnekamskneftekhim, part of the Sibur holding and one of Russia's largest producers of synthetic rubber and plastics, located about 1,200 kilometres from Ukraine. At TAIF-NK, the General Staff said the strike hit the plant's sole primary oil processing unit, known as ELOU-AVT-7, and a fire was reported at the site; the facility processes heavy, high sulphur crude and supplies fuel, petrochemical feedstock and military needs. Nizhnekamsk Mayor Radmir Belyaev said the city came under a prolonged drone attack that damaged industrial facilities and an apartment building, residents were evacuated and several people were injured, with regional authorities reporting three people wounded. Russia's defence ministry said it shot down 533 Ukrainian drones overnight over a dozen regions and annexed Crimea, and a separate strike the same night hit electrical substations in Taganrog, in the Rostov region, killing a chief engineer. The extent of damage at both Nizhnekamsk facilities was still being assessed, the General Staff said.

Ukraine's General Staff said in a Telegram statement that its forces attacked Lukoil's Volgograd refinery overnight into Nov 13, causing a fire, Bloomberg reported via Rigzone on Nov 13. The statement said the plant's four primary processing units, a hydrotreatment unit, six storage tanks and a loading rack were damaged. The refinery, about 900 kilometres southeast of Moscow, has nameplate processing capacity of about 300,000 barrels of crude a day. The strike made Volgograd the ninth Russian oil refinery Ukraine has attacked since the start of November, including the Omsk facility, the country's largest, according to a Bloomberg tally based on statements from officials in both nations and people familiar with the incidents, and the nine plants together carry nameplate capacity of around 2.6 million barrels a day on Bloomberg calculations. How much Volgograd processing has stopped, and for how long, had not been confirmed by the operator in the reporting here.

Four people were killed and two injured in a Ukrainian drone attack on an industrial zone in Russia's southern city of Volgograd, regional governor Andrei Bocharov said on Friday, Nov 13, Reuters reported, calling it the deadliest attack on the city so far. Volgograd is home to a large oil refinery run by Lukoil, which has a processing capacity of approximately 14 million tonnes of crude oil per year, or 280,000 barrels per day, about 5 percent of total refining volume in Russia, according to Lukoil's website cited by Reuters. Unverified video posted on social media purported to show a large fire at the refinery, which has been attacked several times before, and residents reported loud explosions overnight, but there was no official confirmation that the refinery had been attacked and Lukoil did not reply to a request for comment. Ukraine has sharply stepped up its attacks on Russian oil refineries since the end of October, when an energy ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump failed to take hold, Reuters said.

The huge fire that erupted on Nov 11 at Russia's largest Baltic Sea port of Ust-Luga following a Ukrainian overnight drone attack has been contained, but attempts to extinguish it continue, Leningrad region governor Alexander Drozdenko said, Ports Europe reported on Nov 12. Ust-Luga is Russia's second largest port behind Novorossiysk on the Black Sea, handles 700,000 barrels of crude oil per day, and exported more than 32.8 million tonnes of refined oil products last year, Ports Europe said. The port loads crude oil and petroleum products, coal, fertilisers and grain, and is home to the major Novatek refinery; earlier attacks on its oil terminals also caused temporary halts in loadings.

Ukraine's Special Operations Forces (SSO) confirmed they conducted an eight hour drone attack on Russia's largest oil refinery in the Siberian city of Omsk on Nov 11, more than 1,550 miles from the Ukrainian border, the National Security Journal reported on Nov 12. The SSO said the attack was the farthest reaching drone strike conducted by Ukraine on an oil refinery in Russia, with drones flying around 1,864 miles to strike the facility. Residents reported explosions, power cuts and fires at the Gazprom Neft refinery, and Russian officials confirmed a drone attack, but not whether the refinery was struck; there has been no confirmation of damage to specific refining units, and the level of damage remained unclear on Thursday, Nov 12. The refinery can process more than 21 million metric tons of crude oil each year.

The Russian city of Omsk, home to the largest oil refinery in the country, came under sustained drone fire for more than eight hours on Nov 11, EuropeSays reported, republishing reporting by the Kyiv Independent. Omsk Governor Vitaly Khotsenko reported during the day on Nov 11 that Ukrainian drones were attacking the region and urged residents to remain indoors, and residents reported a fire near the Omsk oil refinery, the independent Russian Telegram channel Astra reported, whose open-source analysis confirmed a blaze near the site. The precise targets and the extent of the damage were not yet clear, Khotsenko said emergency workers had been dispatched to sites hit by falling drone debris without specifying which facilities were struck, and residents also reported blackouts in some districts. The Omsk refinery, owned by Gazprom, has a processing capacity of more than 21 million metric tons of crude a year and accounts for about one in every six liters of Russian gasoline and diesel; Ukrainian forces struck the refinery twice before, in July and again in October 2026. The Kyiv Independent could not verify the claims at the time of publication.

Ukraine's General Staff confirmed its drones struck the port of Ust-Luga in Leningrad Oblast overnight into Nov 11, SAGIRE reported on Nov 11. The General Staff said the strikes damaged five oil tanks with a total volume of 150,000 cubic meters, a hydrocracking unit, an air-cooling unit and a pumping station; Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) said the same operation hit the Naro-Fominsk, a Buyan-M class missile boat carrying Onyx and Kalibr missiles. Leningrad Oblast Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko confirmed the attack and said 150 Ukrainian drones were shot down in the region, with three workers injured. The damage figures are Ukrainian military claims and had not been independently verified in the reporting here; the fire, the injuries and the power station shutdown at Ust-Luga were reported separately by Reuters on Nov 11 in this section.

A drone attack caused a fire in the port area of Ust-Luga on the Baltic Sea early on Wednesday, Nov 11, injuring three workers, Leningrad region Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said on Telegram, Reuters reported. Drozdenko said a power station was also cut off as a result of the attack, and that 150 drones were shot down over the Leningrad region in the course of the attack, up from an earlier count of 92 drones downed early on Wednesday reported by Reuters. Ust-Luga is a major oil, oil products and grain export outlet, and the Leningrad region is also home to the Kirishi oil refinery, Russia's second-largest, which was struck on Monday, Nov 9. The Baltic states of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia warned of a drone threat on Wednesday, and Finland adopted temporary partial airspace and maritime curbs amid the attack. Reuters could not immediately independently confirm the report, and whether oil loading at Ust-Luga was interrupted was not established in the reporting here.

Satellite data from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Fire Information for Resource Management System showed many new heat anomalies across the whole Ust-Luga port area on Wednesday, Nov 11, potentially indicating multiple fires, OilPrice.com reported. Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said a preliminary investigation indicated the drone attack struck the port area and sparked a fire, that efforts to extinguish the fire were underway, and that a transformer substation in Ust-Luga also experienced an emergency shutdown. Ust-Luga, the top Russian port for exports of oil and other commodities from the Baltic Sea, has been targeted multiple times by Ukraine, OilPrice.com said, and the attack came as Russia and Ukraine continued US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi.

Drones struck the industrial zone of Kirishi in Leningrad Oblast overnight into Nov 9 and set the KINEF refinery (Kirishinefteorgsintez) ablaze, the Baltic Security Monitor reported. Leningrad Oblast Governor Alexander Drozdenko confirmed impacts in the industrial zone and debris damage to an apartment in town, from which a family was evacuated, with no injuries reported in Kirishi; his count of downed drones rose during the morning from 81 to 113 as the attack was still under way. The independent Russian outlet ASTRA, after analysis of local video, confirmed the fire is at the KINEF refinery itself, and NASA's FIRMS satellite fire monitoring system detected multiple thermal hotspots at the site, the Kyiv Independent reported. Damage to primary crude distillation units, flagged as preliminary by Ukrainian monitoring channels, and any halt in processing and its duration had not been confirmed by independent sources, and the operator had not commented. KINEF, owned by Surgutneftegas and under US sanctions, is one of Russia's three largest refineries, with capacity of roughly 20 million tonnes a year, about 100 kilometres southeast of St. Petersburg and some 800 kilometres from Ukraine's border. It last stopped all processing after the Aug 30, 2026 attack, when two of its primary distillation units were damaged; this is the first strike on the plant since August.

Follow-up on the Saratov strike: Ukrainian drones hit Rosneft's Saratov oil refinery overnight into Nov 7, where several separate fires were observed across the site, Defense Magazine reported on Nov 7, citing the monitoring resource Exilenova+ and Militarnyi. The same night, a missile strike hit the Proton plant in Oryol, which produces optoelectronics and semiconductor components used in Russian military systems; a fire was reported near Building No. 48, and Militarnyi reported Flamingo cruise missiles were likely involved, a detail not officially confirmed. Defense Magazine put Saratov's design capacity at around 7 million tonnes of oil a year, producing gasoline, diesel, marine fuel and bitumen, and said Militarnyi reported the refinery was last struck on Sep 11. No official assessment of damage to either site or of any impact on Saratov's operations had been published in the reporting here.

Ukrainian strike drones attacked the Saratov oil refinery in Russia overnight into Nov 7, EuropeSays reported, republishing reporting by the Kyiv Independent. Local residents reported explosions and monitoring channels released footage of a massive fire in the vicinity of the plant, with preliminary reports of several fires on the refinery premises. The monitoring channel Exilenova+ published video from across Saratov showing the glow over the industrial area. The Saratov refinery, owned by Rosneft, can process around 7 million tonnes of crude oil a year, about 2 to 3 percent of Russia's total refining capacity, and produces petrol, diesel and other products, some used to support Russian military logistics. It is not yet possible to determine from the video the number of hits, the exact location of the fires or the damage to plant equipment, and no official assessment of the damage or of the impact on the refinery's operations had been published at the time of reporting. The plant has been attacked repeatedly in 2026, including a confirmed strike on Sep 11 that damaged a primary crude processing unit and a section of the main pipeline.

Ukrainian drones struck the Afipsky oil refinery in Russia's Krasnodar Krai overnight into Nov 6, EuropeSays reported, republishing Kyiv Post reporting. Air raid sirens sounded across Krasnodar Krai shortly after 1 a.m. local time and residents reported loud explosions; the Krasnodar airport temporarily restricted arrivals and departures. The Krasnodar Krai operational headquarters confirmed a fire broke out at an enterprise in the settlement of Afipsk after falling drone debris, with no casualties, but did not identify the facility; the independent outlet Astra reported its open-source analyst had established from eyewitness photographs that the refinery's reservoir park was on fire, and the monitoring channels Exilenova+ and Exile+ reported a fire with the Afipsky refinery in the background. Krasnodar Krai Governor Veniamin Kondratyev had not officially confirmed an attack on the refinery, Kyiv Post could not independently verify the reports, and Russia's defence ministry said air defences intercepted and destroyed 142 Ukrainian drones overnight over nine regions and the Black and Azov seas. A Reuters wire item the same day reported a fire at an industrial facility in Afipsky following a drone attack, citing the local emergency service, and noted the town hosts the Afipsky refinery. The plant is one of the largest in southern Russia, with annual crude-processing capacity of about 7.2 million tonnes, producing gasoline, diesel, gas condensate distillates, heavy oil residues and sulfur; the extent of any damage has not been established.

Reuters video analysis indicated the Ryazan oil refinery, one of Russia's largest, came under attack as part of a large drone strike overnight into Nov 5 on industrial sites in the city southeast of Moscow, Reuters reported on Nov 5. If confirmed, Ryazan would be the second refinery hit this week, after the Yaroslavl plant northeast of Moscow overnight into Nov 3, marking the breakdown of a pause in strikes. Ryazan's governor said the city had restored power by Thursday as fires at the unnamed industrial sites were contained or put out. Reuters said Ukraine's strikes on oil refineries this year forced large amounts of processing capacity in western Russia offline and caused fuel shortages that led Moscow to enforce fuel export bans from April onwards; a ban on diesel exports has since been lifted in part under the October US-Russia deal to resume diesel exports to international markets. The extent of damage at Ryazan has not been established.

Ukrainian drones struck the Ryazan refinery overnight into Nov 5, the fifth hit on Russian oil refining in seven days, the Baltic Security Monitor reported on Nov 5. Ryazan governor Pavel Malkov said more than 200 drones targeted the region; debris damaged power lines, cutting electricity to parts of the city, fires broke out at industrial sites and one person was injured. Russian media reported a blaze at the Ryazan refinery, and the independent outlet Astra reported a strike on a large Wildberries logistics centre. The governor did not name the facilities hit, and neither Rosneft nor Wildberries has commented. The Ryazan refinery belongs to Rosneft, processes more than 17 million tonnes of crude a year, and supplies petrol, diesel and jet fuel to Moscow and central Russia; one of its primary crude units was shut down after a strike on Oct 15. Russia's Defence Ministry said it downed 496 Ukrainian drones over 13 regions, Crimea and the Black and Azov Seas, a figure the monitor said has not been independently verified. The monitor's week in sequence is Novokuibyshevsk on Oct 30, Ufa on Oct 31, Kstovo overnight into Nov 1, Yaroslavl on Nov 3 and Ryazan on Nov 5, and it cautioned that without satellite imagery or operator data the scale of damage at Ryazan cannot be assessed.

Follow-up on Nov 4: the Baltic Security Monitor, in its Nov 4 security watch, said the independent channel Astra counted at least seven fire sites at the Slavneft-YANOS refinery in Yaroslavl after the overnight strike into Nov 3, and that Governor Mikhail Yevrayev confirmed damage to plant infrastructure and two injured workers, while claiming 124 drones shot down, a figure the monitor said is unverified. The monitor said Russia's Defence Ministry claimed 709 Ukrainian drones intercepted overnight, also without independent confirmation; that total differs from the 856 figure carried in Reuters reporting of the same night, and neither total is independently confirmed. The YANOS strike is confirmed by Russian regional authorities, the monitor said; production losses have not been established, and measured refining impact and satellite imagery are the next checks. YANOS is Russia's fifth-largest refinery, with capacity of up to 15 million tonnes of crude a year, about 250 kilometres from Moscow.

Ukraine set fire to a major oil refinery in the Russian city of Yaroslavl in an overnight drone attack into Nov 3, Reuters reported, citing regional governor Mikhail Yevrayev. The Slavneft Yaroslavnefteorgsintez (YANOS) refinery, which Ukraine has struck at least twice before, disrupting production, is located some 250 kilometres northeast of Moscow and has a processing capacity of around 15 million tons of crude oil per year, producing gasoline, diesel and fuel oil. Yevrayev said air defence forces had repelled an attack on the refinery involving 124 drones and that two employees had been injured, adding that there has been damage to the refinery's infrastructure and that emergency services were working to extinguish a fire. Russia's military said it had downed 856 enemy drones across the country overnight.
