Unverified footage posted on social media showed big flames rising into a darkened sky and what appeared to be two smaller fires, and there was no immediate comment from Ukraine. Reuters noted that Ukraine had paused its strikes on Russian refineries after pressure from US President Donald Trump, according to the Wall Street Journal, but that a Russian official said on Friday that Ukraine had resumed strikes with attacks on three oil refineries and one gas-chemical complex in the Samara region.

Follow-up on Nov 3: the Yaroslavl strike is the third officially acknowledged damage to a Yaroslavl refinery in three months, the Baltic Security Monitor reported, after a 93-drone raid on Aug 6 that struck storage tanks and injured four people and a 65-drone attack on Sep 17 that damaged the refinery with no casualties. The monitor said the Nov 3 statement does not name the facility; the city's largest plant, Slavneft-YANOS, jointly controlled by Rosneft and Gazprom Neft, processes about 15 million tonnes a year, roughly 300,000 barrels per day. Which units were affected this time, primary distillation, storage tanks or auxiliary infrastructure, has not been established, and the monitor cautioned that a fire and two casualties are not the same as lost capacity: in August and September the fires were put out within hours, and without satellite imagery, operator statements or throughput data, claims of a production halt would be premature. Debris also damaged apartment blocks, private homes and cars, and the road out of the city toward Moscow was temporarily closed.

Ukrainian drones struck one of Europe's largest oil transport hubs in Russia's Samara region overnight into Nov 2, EuropeSays reported, citing independent media, as local authorities confirmed the overnight attack without detailing damage or casualties. Samara region governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said early on Nov 2 that air defence systems were repelling an air barrage, and Samara's Kurumoch International Airport temporarily suspended flights for two hours during the air raid alert. The exiled news outlet Astra said it used eyewitness photos of a smoke cloud in Samara to identify at least one targeted facility as Transneft's linear production and dispatch station (LPDS); NASA satellite imagery also showed a large black plume of smoke rising in the area of the site, southeast of the regional capital. The station spans 216 hectares, has 71 storage tanks with a total capacity of 1.6 million cubic metres, and receives crude from Western Siberia, the republic of Tatarstan, the Orenburg region and Kazakhstan via four pipelines before routing it toward two refineries and the Druzhba export pipeline. The attack marks the fifth drone strike on the station after reported strikes on Oct 2, 7, 10 and 11. Russia's Defense Ministry said it intercepted 212 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Sunday evening and Monday morning.

Follow-up on Nov 1: Nizhny Novgorod governor Gleb Nikitin has admitted significant damage to an industrial enterprise in the Kstovo district without naming it, the Baltic Security Monitor reported in a Nov 1 update, upgrading the overnight incident to material status on official acknowledgement carried by Reuters and AFP. The monitor said the identification of the Lukoil-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez (NORSI) refinery remains provisional and lost output is not established, with no Lukoil statement, no independent satellite imagery and no data on unit operations. After an emergency operational meeting, regional authorities urged drivers to refuel only as needed and not to stockpile; Nizhny Novgorod petrol stations were reported running an odd-even scheme based on the last digit of the licence plate, with queues at many chain stations and a fuel-availability service showing some stations low or out of petrol at 13:22 on Nov 1, while officials insisted stocks are sufficient. The monitor noted Kstovo is the third refinery hit within days, after Novokuibyshevsk and Ufa, and cited Russian outlet Agentstvo estimating the three plants together account for about 10 percent of Russian refining and more than 10 percent of its diesel, with its method not disclosed, so the figure is a guide rather than a measurement.

A major Russian oil refinery in Kstovo, in the Nizhny Novgorod region, was reportedly targeted in a drone attack overnight into Nov 1, Euronews reported. Regional governor Gleb Nikitin said in a post on Telegram that a massive UAV attack had resulted in significant damage to an industrial facility in the Kstovsky district, that more than 100 drones had been destroyed, and that early information suggested there had been no casualties, with emergency crews working at the scene. Nikitin said that while restoration work is underway there may be temporary power cuts and reduced hot water and heating supplies in parts of the local utility networks. Telegram war monitoring channels said the attack targeted the Kstovo oil refinery, also known as the Lukoil-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez refinery, thought to be one of Russia's largest such facilities; according to Lukoil, the site produces diesel and aviation fuel, among other products. The reported strike is the third on a Russian refinery in three days, after Novokuibyshevsk on Oct 30 and Ufa on Oct 31.

The Bashneft-Novoil oil refinery in Ufa, in central Russia, caught fire on Oct 31 after a reported Ukrainian drone attack, the Kyiv Independent reported, citing Russian outlet ASTRA's open-source analysis of eyewitness photos, a day after Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian refineries following a two-week pause. A key catalytic reforming unit, the L-35, was likely burning, ASTRA's analyst said; the unit produces reformate, a high-octane gasoline component, and hydrogen needed to refine motor fuels. Residents reported several explosions on the morning of Oct 31, a column of smoke and internet disruptions after a drone alert overnight, and residents claimed two plants were hit, with Telegram channel Exilenova+ reporting fires at two of the three refineries in Ufa's northern industrial zone. Rosneft-owned Bashneft operates three adjacent refineries in Ufa, Bashneft-Ufaneftekhim, Bashneft-Novoil and Bashneft-UNPZ, forming one of Russia's largest refining complexes, with a combined capacity of 23.5 million tons of crude a year, according to ASTRA. Bashneft-Novoil produces Euro-6 gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and industrial oils.

Drones struck Rosneft's Novokuybyshevsk oil refinery in Russia's Samara region early on Oct 30, setting off a large fire, SOFX reported, a day after the Wall Street Journal reported Kyiv had agreed to halt attacks on Russian refineries under pressure from President Donald Trump. Ukrainian drone maker Fire Point said its FP-1 long-range drones scored numerous hits across the plant, including on a unit that removes sulfur from diesel fuel, and the Telegram monitoring channel Exilenova+ counted at least 11 separate fires. Samara governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said Kyiv had launched a record number of drones, that no one was hurt, and asked residents not to reveal what had been hit; Russia's Defence Ministry said air defences shot down 1,043 drones across 19 regions, Samara among them, during the night. The strike was the first reported on a Russian refinery in nearly two weeks; the last documented attacks on Russia's oil sector before it hit the Ryazan refinery on Oct 15 and an industrial site in Surgut on Oct 16. The Novokuybyshevsk refinery, owned by Rosneft since 2007, refines roughly 8.8 million metric tons of crude a year and makes diesel, gasoline and jet fuel for Russia's Aerospace Forces; Ukrainian drones struck it on Aug 22 and on Apr 18, when damage forced both of its main crude-processing units offline.

The same overnight wave on Oct 29-30 also hit a food production plant in Russia's Bryansk region that supplies canned rations to Russian forces, and prompted temporary flight restrictions at all four major Moscow airports, SOFX reported. Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 862 drones had flown toward the Moscow region, with 170 downed as they neared the capital. Neither the Bryansk plant nor the airport closures is a refinery target.

A major fire reportedly broke out at the Novokuybyshevsk oil refinery in Russia's Samara region on Oct 30 following a drone attack, Euronews reported. Russian Telegram channels said a blaze had started at the refinery after a drone warning and a series of explosions, and images and video footage circulating on social media appeared to show multiple columns of black smoke over the complex. The reported strike is the first on a Russian oil refinery in nearly two weeks, landing a day after the Wall Street Journal reported that Ukraine had paused refinery strikes amid pressure from Washington, with the pause expected to last until after the US midterm elections on Nov 3. The Novokuybyshevsk refinery, owned by Rosneft since 2007, can process around 8.8 million tonnes of crude oil per year and is involved in the production of jet fuel. Euronews described the story as developing, with the extent of any damage not yet established.

A Ukrainian drone attack reportedly struck the Bashkir Soda Company chemical plant in Sterlitamak, in Russia's Republic of Bashkortostan, on the morning of Oct 29, with thick white smoke seen rising from the facility, UNITED24 Media reported via EuropeSays, citing Russian media outlet ASTRA. Russian authorities acknowledged damage at an industrial plant after eight drones attacked the city, and open-source geolocation placed the smoke inside the Bashkir Soda complex. The plant is one of Russia's largest chemical complexes, producing soda ash, polyvinyl chloride and other industrial chemicals, and is reportedly the only Russian producer of terephthaloyl chloride, a compound used in high-strength aramid fibres for ballistic protection. The target is a chemical plant, not an oil refinery.

A Ukrainian open-source intelligence assessment published on Oct 28 gave updated battle damage assessments for Ukraine's Oct 24 strikes in Omsk, EuropeSays reported. The assessment confirmed damage to gas separation and final production units at the Omskiy Kauchuk chemical plant, to finished product lines and pipelines at the Poliom polypropylene plant, and to two sections of an Ozon warehouse facility in Omsk, roughly 2,500 kilometres from the Ukrainian border. The targets are petrochemical and logistics facilities, not the Gazprom Neft Omsk refinery.

Fires were reported overnight on Oct 27-28 at the Novolipetsk Steel Plant (NLMK), Russia's largest steel producer, and at the Azot chemical plant in Novomoskovsk in the Tula region, following a large wave of Ukrainian drone attacks, EuropeSays reported citing the Kyiv Post. Lipetsk governor Igor Artamonov said 45 drones were shot down over the region and that reports of a major fire at an industrial facility were not true, saying drone debris fell in a wooded area and sparked a contained fire. Tula governor Dmitry Milyaev said drone debris in Novomoskovsk damaged an apartment building, private homes and infrastructure in the adjacent industrial zone, without identifying the facility targeted; the monitoring channel Exilenova+ and the Russian outlet Astra identified the target as the EuroChem Azot plant, one of Russia's largest nitrogen fertiliser producers. Moscow said air defences intercepted and destroyed 531 Ukrainian drones overnight, a figure not independently verified, and Kyiv had not commented on the attacks. Neither target is an oil refinery.

A drone attack in Russia's Voronezh region killed two men and injured 17 people, including a child, regional governor Alexander Gusev said on Oct 26, Reuters reported. Air defence systems had destroyed 113 drones over the region, Gusev wrote on the MAX messaging app. Fires also broke out at several industrial sites, Gusev said. A passenger train bound for Moscow from Anapa was also damaged and five passengers injured, Russian Railways said, and train services through Voronezh have been suspended. Reuters could not independently verify the report. No refinery was named among the targets in the Reuters reporting.

A chemical plant producing dual-use goods in Voronezh was likely hit in the Oct 26 Ukrainian drone attack, independent Russian media outlet Astra said, in reporting by the Kyiv Independent via EuropeSays. Astra cited videos taken by local residents showing black smoke rising over the territory of the plant, known as Voronezhsintezkauchuk, owned by Russia's largest petrochemical company, Sibur; the plant produces over 385,000 metric tons of synthetic rubbers and thermoplastic elastomers per year. Governor Gusev said fires broke out at several unspecified industrial facilities without serious consequences. Neither Ukrainian nor Russian officials have confirmed the attack on Voronezhsintezkauchuk, Ukrainian defence company Fire Point claimed its FP-1 deep-strike drones had been used, and the Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claim. The target is a petrochemical plant, not an oil refinery.

Ukrainian long-range drones struck the Omsky Kauchuk petrochemical plant and an Ozon logistics warehouse in Omsk on Oct 24, more than 2,500 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, UNITED24 Media reported via EuropeSays. Omsky Kauchuk, part of the Titan Group, is one of Russia's largest producers of synthetic rubber and also makes methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE), a gasoline additive, as well as phenol and acetone, and Ukrainian reporting links the plant to the supply chain for rocket fuel including for the Iskander ballistic missile. Footage circulated by the monitoring community Exilenova+ showed a large fire at the plant, Omsk regional governor Vitaly Khotsenko confirmed drones had reached the city's northern industrial district and that a logistics hub was attacked with personnel evacuated, and the extent of damage and any impact on production had not been independently verified. The Omsk target is a petrochemical plant, not the Gazprom Neft Omsk refinery struck on Oct 8.

Several industrial facilities were damaged in a drone attack on the Russian city of Togliatti on Oct 24, local authorities said, while Ukraine said it had struck a major petrochemical plant there, Reuters reported. Togliatti mayor Ilya Sukhikh said preliminary reports indicated no fatalities or injuries and did not specify which facilities had been hit. Ukraine's General Staff said it had struck the Togliattikauchuk petrochemical plant, one of Russia's largest producers of synthetic rubber, and also reported a strike on the Proton electronics plant in Russia's Oryol region, which Kyiv says manufactures components for cruise and ballistic missiles. Oryol regional governor Andrei Klychkov said three people were killed on Oct 23 in a Ukrainian missile strike on an unspecified civilian facility in the region. Ukraine's military also reported hitting an aircraft at the Yeysk airfield in southern Russia, where local authorities confirmed an attack but said it caused only minor damage to two apartment buildings. Russia's Defence Ministry said on Oct 24 that air defences had destroyed 1,297 drones, one French-made SCALP cruise missile and four Ukrainian Neptune missiles over the previous 24 hours.

Rosneft is deliberately slowing repairs at most of its damaged refineries, stretching work that could be completed in days into months, Bloomberg reported on Oct 22 via investingLive. Refineries that Rosneft restarted within weeks of an attack were hit again as repairs neared completion, wiping out the investment, and company officials have privately warned the costs cannot be sustained and that a few more months of war could inflict catastrophic and lasting damage across the business. Ukraine's defence ministry said earlier in October that strikes had knocked out about half of Russia's refining capacity, a figure it acknowledged could not be independently verified, and Goldman Sachs estimated Russian refinery outages are about 3 million b/d higher than a year ago. Bloomberg calculations based on Vortexa data showed Russia's seaborne fuel exports fell to about 980,000 b/d in the first 10 days of October before the government relaxed some export restrictions.

Drones launched a massive attack on the Moscow region overnight on Oct 22, with the 75 Arsenal military plant in Serpukhov among the targets, EuropeSays reported citing The Moscow Times via Ukrinform. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 630 drones had been heading toward Moscow since the evening of Oct 21, 163 of which were shot down during the attack on the city, and two people were injured in the area of the village of Voronovo. According to Astra, drones attacked the 75 Arsenal plant and footage recorded by eyewitnesses showed an explosion and fire at the facility following the drone strikes. No refinery hit was confirmed in this report.
claims.source: EuropeSays (citing The Moscow Times via Ukrinform)

claims.text: Satellite imagery published on Oct 20 indicates that Ukraine's Oct 10 strike against the NZNP oil-loading terminal in Rostov Oblast damaged eight oil storage tanks, each with a capacity of 5,000 cubic metres, the Institute for the Study of War assessment for Oct 21 reported via EuropeSays. The terminal loads petroleum products from the Novoshakhtinsk refinery onto river-sea tankers for export.
claims.source: EuropeSays (citing Institute for the Study of War)

claims.text: A fire broke out at an oil pumping station near Michurinsk in Russia's Tambov Oblast after an overnight drone attack on Oct 20, according to Telegram monitoring channels reported by the Kyiv Independent via EuropeSays. Tambov Oblast Governor Yevgeny Pervyshov said a Ukrainian drone attack caused a fire on the territory of one of the enterprises in Michurinsky District without naming the facility, claimed four drones were shot down, and reported no casualties. Independent Russian outlet ASTRA said the fire likely started at the Nikolskoye-1 linear production and dispatch station near Novonikolskoye, a Transneft facility on the Druzhba pipeline network about 350 to 400 kilometres from the front line, which Ukraine previously attacked on Aug 18, 2025, when the strike halted Druzhba operation. Ukrainian authorities did not confirm the attack and the Kyiv Independent could not independently verify a fire at the station.

Reports on Oct 20 confirmed the damage from the Oct 17-18 Ukrainian drone attack on St. Petersburg, Tank Storage Magazine reported: at the St. Petersburg oil terminal, three storage tanks caught fire, with two damaged and one completely destroyed; at the Ruchyi oil depot, one vertical steel tank was destroyed and another damaged. A large scale fire at the Ozon logistics hub affected more than 10,000 square metres, and the Southern Fairway Bridge and the Finland Railway Bridge were both damaged. One person was confirmed killed and 15 others injured in the overall attack, which involved over 1,000 drones launched at the terminal, the depot, the logistics hub and the bridges.

The St. Petersburg oil terminal struck on Oct 18 exports about 120,000 b/d of refined products, mostly fuel oil, according to data from Kpler cited by CNBC on Oct 19, and it is unclear how bad the damage at the facility is. Ukraine briefly paused strikes on Russian energy facilities after President Trump declared on Oct 11 that Kyiv and Moscow had agreed to a truce, but Russia continued to strike Ukrainian energy infrastructure after that announcement and President Zelenskiy said last week Kyiv would resume strikes on Russian facilities in retaliation.

Ukraine launched one of the largest drone attacks of the war overnight Oct 17-18, striking the St. Petersburg oil terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot, with fires also reported at industrial warehouses in the city's Kolpinsky District, St. Petersburg governor Alexander Beglov said. One person was killed and five injured in St. Petersburg, and two transformer substations struck at Yanino in the Leningrad region left about 20,000 people without electricity on Sunday morning. Russia's Defence Ministry said air defences shot down some 1,015 drones near Moscow and several other western regions.

Reuters reported on Oct 16, citing unnamed industry sources, that Rosneft's Ryazan refinery suspended operations at one of its main crude distillation units, CDU-6, following the drone attack on Oct 15. The same unit had already been shut after a drone strike in September. The refinery's three other primary crude distillation units, CDU-1, CDU-3 and CDU-4, reportedly continue to operate.

A large Ukrainian drone attack caused a fire at Rosneft's Ryazan refinery early on Oct 15, regional governor Pavel Malkov said, with damage still being assessed and emergency services at the scene. The plant, about 300 km southeast of Moscow, supplies fuel to the capital and accounts for almost 5 percent of Russian refining throughput; it has been hit several times in recent months.

Ukraine's Ministry of Defence said its forces hit 12 large Russian refineries in September, per ArmyInform reporting on Oct 12, with Lukoil's Perm refinery, about 1,500 km from the border, the farthest on the list. Monitoring by Euromaidan Press found no reports of new Ukrainian refinery strikes in the sources it tracks since the Oct 11 ceasefire announcement.

Ukraine's military confirmed long-range drones struck Tatneft's TANECO refinery at Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan on Oct 12, about 750 miles from the Ukrainian border, as part of a wider attack on industrial targets in the region. Tatarstan's leader said the attack killed at least 13 people, including a child, and wounded 39. TANECO processed 17 million tons of crude in 2024, producing 2.7 million tons of gasoline and 8.5 million tons of diesel, and had been hit before in early June.

Three of Russia's six largest diesel-producing refineries are now shut or running at roughly one-quarter capacity, according to Reuters calculations cited Oct 12: Kirishi is completely offline, Volgograd and NORSI are at about 25 percent of nameplate, and TANECO was struck on Sunday Oct 11. The six plants, Omsk, Kirishi, TANECO, Volgograd, NORSI and Perm, together account for roughly half of Russian diesel production.

Ukraine struck the Samara linear production and dispatch station, a Transneft Urals-blend hub, for the third time this month overnight Oct 9-10; the Ukrainian General Staff said the earlier Oct 2 and Oct 7 hits caused extensive damage to storage tanks and associated infrastructure at the junction.

Ukrainian drones struck the Novoshakhtinsk/Yug Rusi oil-loading terminal in Rostov-on-Don overnight Oct 9-10, starting a major fire at the export-loading facility; the regional governor confirmed two ships damaged at the Port of Azov and a rail bridge strike in the same wave.

Ukraine attacked Lukoil's Ukhta oil-processing plant in the Komi Republic, the fourth Russian refinery hit this week after Omsk, Salavat and the Astrakhan gas plant, President Zelenskyy confirmed Friday; the plant's design capacity is about 80,000 b/d, and Bloomberg calculates the four facilities hit this week total about 720,000 b/d of crude capacity plus up to 12 Bcm per year of gas.

Ukraine's General Staff said it struck Russia's largest refinery, the Gazprom Neft Omsk plant (about 440,000 b/d, roughly one-fifteenth of national capacity), overnight Oct 8, some 2,500-2,700 km from Ukraine; regional governor Vitaly Khotsenko confirmed a drone hit an industrial zone. It is the second strike on Omsk since July 6, and Zelenskyy called it an 'important achievement,' saying 'Siberia, too, is now within reach.'

In the same overnight wave, Ukraine's military said it struck the Ust-Luga and Vysotsk ports, which handle Baltic Sea oil exports, plus targets in the Kaluga and Yaroslavl regions, with local governors confirming the attacks; the strikes widen the campaign from refineries to export infrastructure.

Ukraine's General Staff confirmed on Oct 8 that the Oct 2 strike on the Samara linear production and dispatch station at Prosvet damaged 11 RVS-20000 tanks, 3 RVS-50000 tanks, pipeline sections and an automated oil loading station; the hub blends Urals export crude and, per the General Staff, handles up to half of Russia's oil exports.

Ukraine's General Staff claimed an overnight strike on the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat refinery complex in Bashkortostan, described as one of Russia's largest oil refining and petrochemical facilities, about 750 miles east of Moscow; local authorities had not confirmed the claim. The 200 kb/d plant was previously hit on July 14 and September 24, when its AVT-6 primary unit caught fire.

President Zelenskyy said on Oct 7 that Ukrainian forces struck two oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions over the past day, calling them 'justified responses' to Russian strikes on Ukraine.

Rosneft's Ryazan refinery, Russia's fourth-largest at more than 260,000 b/d, suspended crude processing after a weekend drone attack; Reuters industry sources said the plant is expected to stay idle until the end of the month with no product loadings planned before Dec 1, and a second crude unit is under repair after an earlier strike that took about 80,000 b/d offline.

Overnight on Oct 5-6, Ukraine launched what Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin called one of the largest drone attacks on the capital region in two years, with about 650 drones approaching and 105 downed near the city; the regional governor reported one fatality and six injured. Monitoring channels and eyewitness footage showed flames and heavy smoke at the Volodarskaya linear production and dispatch station near Konstantinovo, Transneft's largest Moscow-region oil depot at about 3 million tons a year, which supplies fuel to the capital's three main airports; Russian authorities have not confirmed damage at the depot itself.
claims.source: The Gaze (citing Astra and eyewitness footage)

claims.text: Ukraine's General Staff said a drone strike ignited fires at the port of Taman in the Krasnodar region, damaging an oil storage tank, a warehouse and terminals, with regional governor Veniamin Kondratyev reporting two people wounded. The same statement said a Pantsir-S1 air defense system in occupied Crimea was also hit.

Ukraine's General Staff confirmed the October 1-2 strikes on the Lukoil-Volgogradneftepererabotka refinery, one of Russia's largest at about 15 million tons per year, and on Transneft's Samara tank farm plus the Samara-1 and Samara-2 pumping stations; analysts described the Samara facility as Europe's largest tank farm. Russia's defense ministry claimed to have intercepted 646 drones in the same overnight wave.
Russia's second-largest refinery, Kirishi, halted processing on September 29 after Ukrainian drone attacks damaged three of its four crude distillation units, two industry sources told Reuters.

Russia raised its expected idle primary refining capacity for October by 67% versus the earlier plan to 4.0 million tons, per Reuters industry-source estimates, after postponed maintenance at Rosneft's Novokuibyshevsk refinery and a unit of Lukoil's NORSI; Rosneft's Tuapse refinery also reportedly halted crude processing on Oct 1 on low margins. More than half of October's idle capacity is expected to return in November, with November idle at 1.2 to 1.8 million tons.

The Associated Press reported on Oct 4 that the International Energy Agency estimates a Russian refinery has been successfully struck by a drone roughly once every three days in recent months. The cadence is consistent with a sustained attrition campaign but is not an independent confirmation of Ukraine's claim, which AP noted it could not verify, that 51% of Russian refining capacity is out of action.

Ukraine's Defence Ministry said on October 4 that long-range strikes have put 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity out of action, citing strikes on refineries in Moscow, Yaroslavl, Perm, Saratov and Syzran plus the Kirishi (Kinef) and Ust-Luga plants. The claim could not be independently verified. President Vladimir Putin told the Valdai forum on October 1 that the strikes had cost Russia about 1% of gross domestic product (GDP), while International Energy Agency (IEA) data cited in the report says Russian diesel output has fallen about 30%, with drivers queuing up to 40 hours at filling stations and Moscow banning diesel exports.

Ukraine's Defense Intelligence representative Andrii Yusov said Ukrainian forces have conducted 64 targeted strikes on Russian fuel infrastructure facilities this year, destroying or damaging about one-third of the targeted refineries and storage facilities, and said the strikes compound Western sanctions that restrict imports of repair equipment. The agency framed the disruption as long-term pressure on Russian military logistics. This is a Ukrainian claim, not independently verified.
